newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasury has no comment on Hashimoto remarks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasury has no comment on Hashimoto remarks.

text.p: A Treasury Department official said late on Monday that it had no comment on remarks by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto about the need for U.S. cooperation to keep Japan from "being tempted" to sell U.S. securities.
Hashimoto's remarks, made in response to questions after an address at New York's Columbia University, contributed to a big decline in U.S. markets late on Monday.
Hashimoto said he would like U.S. cooperation in stabilizing foreign exchange rates because currency volatility might cause Japanese authorities to sell holdings of U.S. securities.

Hashimoto did not actually say whether Japan, a major purchaser of U.S. government debt, would sell its U.S. Treasury securities if the dollar fell sharply. But he urged U.S. cooperation in exchange markets "in order to prevent us from being tempted to sell U.S. Treasuries and buy gold."
"We have no comment tonight," the U.S. Treasury official said.

Earlier on Monday, the quarterly Treasury Bulletin reported Japan's net purchases of U.S. Treasury bonds and notes fell to $12.86 billion in the first quarter from $15.44 billion in last year's final quarter.

After Hashimoto's remarks, share prices on the New York Stock Exchange ended down 192.25 points for the biggest loss since "Black Monday" on Oct 19, 1987, when it plummeted 508 points. The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond slid nearly 1/2 of a point with the yield climbing to 6.70 percent from Friday's closing 6.66 percent.
Just last week, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin met Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka in Denver where they agreed to continue closely cooperating against currency fluctuations.

Since then, before and following the summit of the Group of Eight in Denver where the United States, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and Britain were joined by Russia for economic talks, President Clinton has criticized Japan's persistent huge trade surpluses.

Hashimoto pointed out on Monday that Japanese buying of U.S. Treasury securities helps the U.S. economy. If the Japanese government sold its holdings, "such sales might have a big impact on the U.S. economy," the Japanese leader noted.
